{{RunningHeader|thussock|6323|thwart}}'''thussock†''', ''n.'' Same as ''tussock''. '''thuswise''' (ᴛ̵ʜus′wīz), ''adv.'' [< ''thus''1 + ''wise''2.] In this manner; thus. [Rare.] {{smaller block|It is surely better . . . to acquire pieces of historical information ''thuswise'' than never to acquire them at all. {{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XX. 113.}}}} '''Thuya''' (thū′yä̤), ''n.'' [NL. (Tournefort, 1700), < Gr. θυία, θύα, an African tree with sweet-smelling wood, supposed to be a kind of juniper or arbor-vitæ.] A genus of conifers (the arbor-vitæ), of the tribe ''Cupressineæ'' and subtribe ''Thuyopsidinæ.'' {{smaller|It is distinguished from ''Cupressus'', the cypress, by its smaller, less indurated cones, and usually complanate leafy branches. The 4 species are natives of North America and eastern Asia. They are evergreen trees and shrubs with a very characteristic habit, having the flat leaf-like branchlets almost wholly covered by small appressed imbricated leaves, some of which are awl-shaped and slightly spreading; others, on different branchlets, are blunt, scale-like, and adnate. The small ovoid or oblong cone rarely exceeds half an inch in length, and is usually composed of from three to six pairs of coriaceous scales, dry and spreading when ripe, the lowest and uppermost empty, the others bearing two or three seeds each. The typical species, ''T. occidentalis'', the arbor-vitæ, or white cedar, of the northern United States, forms extensive cedar-swamps from Minnesota to central New York and New Brunswick, and occurs on rocky banks and along the mountains to North Carolina. It is usually a small tree, but is sometimes from 50 to 70 feet high. It is cultivated for lawns and hedges, and yields a valuable light-brown wood, a very aromatic oil, and a tincture used as an emmenagogue. ''T. gigantea'', the canoe-cedar, or red cedar, of the West, found chiefly from Alaska to Oregon, is a large tree often from 100 to 135 feet high and 12 feet in diameter. One is said to have measured 22 feet in diameter and 325 in height. The trunk rises often for 100 feet as a columnar shaft free from branches. The trunks were hollowed out by the Indians into canoes. The dull reddish-brown wood—which is light, soft, compact, easily worked, and, as in the other species, slow to decay—is greatly valued for cabinet-work, interior finish, cooperage, etc. The bark yields a fiber which is made into hats, mats, and baskets. In cultivation it is often known by the names of ''T. plicata'' and ''T. Lobbii'', and in Europe as ''Libocedrus decurrens'', by an early exchange with the true ''Libocedrus'', the incense-cedar of California. The other commonly cultivated species, ''T.'' (''Biota'') ''orientalis'', the Chinese arbor-vitæ, native of eastern Asia, is parent of numerous varieties remarkably different in habit, with bright-green, golden, silvery, or variegated spray, closer and more vertical than in the tree of the Atlantic coast, or drooping, elongated, and slightly cylindrical in the variety ''pendula'', the weeping arbor-vitæ. Several other species formerly classed here are now separated, as the genera ''Thuyopsis'' and ''Chamæcyparis''. Compare also ''Retinospora''.}} [[File:century v08 p0127 c1f1.png|center|360px]] {{c|Branch with Cones of American Arbor-vitæ (''Thuya occidentalis'').
''a'', the male flower; ''b'', scale of cone, showing the two seeds; ''c'', a seed, ventral view.}} '''thuyite''' (thū′yīt), ''n.'' [< ''Thuya'' + ''-ite''2.] A fossil plant supposed to belong or be closely related to ''Thuya''. {{smaller|Several plants from the Wealden and Jurassic have been described under ''Thuyites'' as a generic name, in regard to all or most of which there is considerable}} uncertainty. '''Thuyopsidinæ''' (thū-yop-si-dī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL. (Engler, 1887), < ''Thuyopsis'' (''-id-'') + ''-inæ''.] A subtribe of conifers, of the tribe ''Cupressineæ'', typified by the genus ''Thuyopsis'', and comprising also ''Libocedrus'' and ''Thuya''. '''Thuyopsis''' (thū-yop′sis), ''n.'' [NL. (Siebold and Zuccarini, 1842), < ''Thuya'' + Gr. ὄψις, resemblance.] A genus of conifers, of the tribe ''Cupressineæ'', type of the subtribe ''Thuyopsidinæ''. {{smaller|It is characterized by its narrowly two-winged seeds, four or five under each of four to eight fertile scales of the globose cone. The only species, ''T. dolabrata'', is a native of Japan, there known as ''akeki'', and planted to shade avenues. It is a tall conical evergreen from 50 to 90 feet high. Its pendulous whorled primary branches bear very numerous two-ranked branchlets wholly covered by opposite leaves imbricated in four ranks, the marginal ranks larger, acute, and slightly spreading, the others appressed, glandular, and shining. It is cultivated in dwarf varieties as a shrub for lawns, under the name of ''hatchet-leaved arborvitæ.''}} '''thwack''' (thwak), ''v. t.'' [Also dial. ''twack''; a var. of ''whack'', prob. due in part to confusion with the equiv. ''thack''2, and in part to a phonetic interchange, ''wh-'' to ''thw-'', which occurs in the other direction in ''white''2, var. of ''thwite'', in ''whittle'', var. of ''thwittle'', in ''whart'', var. of ''thwart''1, etc.] 1. To strike with something flat or hard; beat; bang; whack. {{smaller block|He shall not stay, We'll ''thwack'' him hence with distaffs. {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., i. 2. 37.}}}} {{smaller block|Take all my cushions down, and ''thwack'' them soundly, After my feast of millers. {{right|''Middleton (and another)'', Mayor of Queenborough, v. 1.}}}} 2†. To ram down; pack. {{smaller block|The letters he addressed me from time to time, to the number of six hundred, ''thwackt'' with loue and kindnesse. {{right|''Stanihurst'', Descrip. of Ireland (Holinshed's Chron., I. 42).}}}} '''thwack''' (thwak), ''n.'' [< ''thwack'', ''v.''] A sharp blow with something flat or hard; a whack; a bang. {{smaller block|But Talgol first with hardy ''thwack'' Twice bruised his head, and twice his back. {{right|''S. Butler'', Hudibras, I. ii. 795.}}}} {{smaller block|Noble captain, lend me a reasonable ''thwack'', for the love of God, with that cane of yours over these poor shoulders. {{right|''Swift'', Tale of a Tub, xi.}}}} {{smaller|='''Syn.''' See ''thump''.}} '''thwacker''' (thwak′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''thwack'' + ''-er''1.] One who or that which thwacks; specifically, a wooden tool used for beating half-dried pantiles into shape. The tiles are then trimmed with a thwacking-knife. '''thwacking''' (thwak′ing), ''a.'' Thumping; tremendous; great. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|''Sec. Ser.'' A bonfire, sir?
''Sir Ol.'' A ''thwacking'' one, I charge you. {{right|''Middleton'', Chaste Maid, v. 3.}}}} '''thwacking-frame''' (thwak′ing-frām), ''n.'' In ''tile-making'', a table with a curved top, on which a half-dried pantile is bent to form by means of blows with a thwacker. ''E. H. Knight.'' '''thwacking-knife''' (thwak′ing-nīf), ''n.'' A knife for trimming pantiles on the thwacking-frame. '''thwaite1''' (thwāt), ''n.'' [Also dial. ''twaite''; < ME. *''thwaite'' (> AF. ''twaite''), < Icel. ''thveit'', f., ''thveiti'', n., a piece or parcel of land, a paddock (common in local names), also a unit of weight, and a small coin, = Norw. ''tveit'', ''tvet'', ''tvedt'', ''tved'', a piece of ground (common in local names), lit. a piece, from the verb seen in AS. ''thwītan'', ME. ''thwiten'', cut, chop: see ''thwite''.] A piece of ground reclaimed and converted to tillage. {{smaller|''Thwaite'' chiefly occurs as the second element in local names, especially in the lake district of the north of England, as in Bassen''thwaite'', Cross''thwaite'', and Stone''thwaite''.}} '''thwaite2''' (thwāt), ''n.'' Same as ''twaite''2. '''thwang†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''thong''. '''thwarle†''', ''a.'' [ME., perhaps connected with ''twirl'' (D. ''dwarlen''); otherwise possibly an error for ''thwart'', cross: see ''thwart''1, ''a.''] Twisted (?); intricate (?): found only in the following passage. {{smaller block|As the dok lasted,
Sythen thrawen wyth a thwong a ''thwarle'' knot alofte,
Ther mony bellez ful bryȝt of brende golde rungen. {{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 194.}}}} '''thwart'''1 (thwârt), ''adv.'' and ''prep.'' [< ME. ''thwert'' (as in ''over thwert, thwert over, a thwert, a thirt'', athwart), < Icel. ''thvert'', across (''um-thvert'', across, athwart), = Sw. ''tvärt'', rudely, = Dan. ''tvert'', adv., across, athwart (cf. MD. ''dwers, dwersch, dwars'', D. ''dwars'' = G. ''zwerch'', across); prop. neut. acc. (with the neut. suffix ''-t'' usual in Scand.) of the adj., Icel. ''thverr'', cross, transverse, = Sw. ''tvär-'' = Dan. ''tver-'' = AS. ''thweorh'' (''thweor-''), transverse, perverse, = MD. *''dwer'', *''dwar'', ''dwers, dwersch, dwars'', D. ''dwars'', adj., = OHG. ''dwerah, twerh'', MHG. ''twerch, dwerch'', also ''querch'', G. ''zwerch'' in comp., also without the final guttural, OHG. ''twer'', MHG. ''twer, quer'', G. ''quer'' = LG. ''quer'' (> E. ''queer''1), cross, transverse, = Goth. ''thwairhs'', angry (not found in lit. sense 'cross'; cf. E. ''cross''1, 'transverse,' also 'angry'); perhaps connected with L. ''torquere'', twist: see ''tort''1. Connection with AS. ''thurh'', Goth. ''thairh'', etc., through, is improbable: see ''thorough, through''1. Cf. ''athwart.''] '''I.''' ''adv.'' From side to side; across; crosswise; transversely; athwart. {{smaller block|Yet, whether ''thwart'' or flatly it did lyte,
The tempred steele did not into his braynepan byte. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. vi. 30.}}}} {{smaller block|The bait was guarded with at least two hundred men, and thirty lying vnder a great tree (that lay ''thwart'' as a barricado). Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith's'' Works, I. 215.}} II. ''prep.'' 1. Across; athwart. {{smaller block|And laying ''thwart'' her horse, In loathly wise like to a carrion corse, She bore him fast away. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. vii. 43.}}}} {{smaller block|Cornelius May and one other going ashore with some goods late in a faire euening, such a sudden gust did arise that driue them ''thwart'' the Riuer. {{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith's'' Works, II. 93.}}}} 2. Opposite to; over against. {{smaller block|The first of April we weighed anchor in the Downs, and, ''thwart'' Dover, we found our men in ketches ready to come aboard. {{right|''Sir H. Middleton'', Voyage, p. 2.}}}} '''thwart'''1 (thwârt), ''a.'' [< ME. ''thwert'', < ''thwert'', ''adv.''; or < Icel. ''thvert'', neut. adj., after the adv.: see ''thwart''1, ''adv.'' The proper mod. form of the adj. would be *''thwar'' (< early ME. ''thweor'', < AS. ''thweor-'', the reduced form in inflection of ''thweorh'') or *''thwarrow'', < AS. ''thweorh''.] 1. Lying or extending across or crosswise; cross; transverse. {{smaller block|Those streetes that be ''thwart'' are faire and large. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', II. 234.}}}} {{smaller block|The slant lightning, whose ''thwart'' flame, driven down, Kindles the gummy bark of fir or pine. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 1075.}}}} 2†. Antithetical. {{smaller block|It is observable that Solomon's proverbial says are so many select aphorisms, containing, for the most part, a pair of cross and ''thwart'' sentences, handled rather by collation than relation, whose conjunction is disjunctive. {{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 216.}}}} 3. Perverse; contrary; cross-grained. {{smaller block|His herte tho wurth ''thwert''. ''Genesis and Exodus'', l. 3099.}} {{smaller block|If she must teem, Create her child of spleen, that it may live And be a ''thwart'' disnatured torment to her! {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4. 305.}} Now he would make that love prevail in the world and become its law; the world, still ''thwart'' and untoward, foils his purpose, and he dies. {{right|''E. Dowden'', Shelley, II. 130.}}}} '''thwart'''1 (thwârt), ''n.'' [< ''thwart''1, ''v.''] Opposition; defiance. {{smaller block|A certain discourteous person, who calleth himself the devil, even now, and in ''thwart'' of your fair inclinations, keepeth and detaineth your irradiant frame in hostile thraldom. {{right|''Miss Burney'', Cecilia, ii. 3.}}}} '''thwart'''1 (thwârt), ''v.'' [< ME. ''thwerten''; < ''thwart''1, ''adv.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To pass over or across; cross. {{smaller block|Pericles
Is now again ''thwarting'' the wayward seas. {{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, iv. 4. 10.}} Swift as a shooting star
In autumn ''thwarts'' the night. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 557.}} In this passage we frequently chang'd our barge, by reason of the bridges ''thwarting'' our course. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 5, 1641.}}}} '''2†.''' To put crosswise, or one across another. {{smaller block|All knights-templars make such Saltire Cross with their ''thwarted'' legs upon their monuments. {{right|''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., III. iii. 11.}}}} '''3†.''' To put in the way; oppose. {{smaller block|'Gainst which the noble sonne of Telamon
Oppos'd himselfe, and, ''thwarting'' his huge shield,
Them battell bad. {{right|''Spenser'', Virgil's Gnat, l. 514.}}}} '''4.''' To cross, as a purpose; contravene; frustrate; baffle. {{smaller block|''Third Out.'' Have you long sojourned there?
''Val.'' Some sixteen months; and longer might have stay'd,
If crooked fortune had not ''thwarted'' me. {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 1. 22.}}}} {{smaller block|The proposals of the one never ''thwarted'' the inclinations of the other. {{right|''South'', Sermons.}}}} {{smaller block|O ''thwart'' me not, sir Soph, at ev'ry turn,
Nor carp at ev'ry flaw you may discern. {{right|''Cowper'', Conversation, l. 91.}}}} {{smaller block|"It is no part of the duty of a Christian Prince," added the Abbess, "to ''thwart'' the wishes of a pious soul." {{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, xxxv.}}}} {{smaller block|No injudicious interference from any quarter ever ''thwarted'' my plans for her [a pupil's] improvement. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xii.}}}} {{smaller|='''Syn.''' 4. ''Foil, Baffle'', etc. See ''frustrate''.}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' 1. To go crosswise or obliquely. ''Thomson.''—2. To be in opposition; be contrary or perverse; hence, to quarrel; contend. {{smaller block|''Thwart'' not thou with thy fellow. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 75.}}}} [Rare in both senses.] '''thwart'''2 (thwârt), ''n.'' [Also dial. ''thought;'' prob. a var. of ''thoft''1 (as, reversely, ''thoft''2 is a var. of ''thought''1), a rower's seat, mixed with ''thwart''1, as if lit. a 'crosspiece': see ''thoft''1, ''thoft-fellow''.] A seat across a boat on which the oarsman sits. {{smaller|A thwart is usually a special fixture, but a board may be used for the purpose. Some thwarts are contrived to slide backward and forward with the movements of the oarsman, as in light sculls or shells used for rowing exercise or for racing.}} {{smaller block|Take care of your dress in the mud — one foot on the ''thwarts'' — sit in the middle — that 's it. {{right|''Whyte Melville'', White Rose, II. vii.}}}}
